last_spoken_paragraph: Some of those journeys are already part of the English we speak.
next_opening: Zero, algebra and algorithm are ordinary English words. They also carry clues about people learning from other languages. In my project Riḥlat al-Kalimāt, the journey of words, I follow clues like these.

last_spoken_paragraph: Looking carefully at earlier lives also has a place in our shared faith.
next_opening: Fa-sīrū fī l-arḍi fa-nẓurū. So travel through the land and look.

last_spoken_paragraph: Caring for that learning brings us to amānah: something placed in our care.
next_opening: Amānah means a trust: something we receive with a responsibility to care for it. Knowledge can be such a trust. We need to understand it well enough to use it carefully and explain it honestly.

last_spoken_paragraph: Let us begin with receiving: why were readers in Baghdad looking for old books, and why were many of them in Greek?
next_opening: Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasids, a Muslim ruling family. By the 9th century, people there were seeking books from several older traditions of learning. They had practical reasons to care. Doctors wanted to understand illness. People needed calculation for trade, land and inheritance. Others wanted to study the sky and the reasons things happen.

last_spoken_paragraph: This medical page lets us see what a Greek work looked like after it became available to Arabic readers.
next_opening: The writing is Arabic, but the work began with a Greek medical author. Dioscorides, a doctor in the 1st century, wrote about materials used as medicines. Later readers translated and studied his book because knowing a name was not enough. They wanted to know what a material was and how it was used.

last_spoken_paragraph: Hunayn left an account of that difficulty: he knew the title of a book he wanted, but finding its pages was another matter.
next_opening: The book was Galen’s On Demonstration. Demonstration here means proof: showing why a conclusion follows from its reasons. Hunayn wanted the complete work, rather than a few pages with a famous name attached.

last_spoken_paragraph: And when better copies did appear, they could change a translation that readers were already using.
next_opening: Hunayn tells us what that meant in another work by Galen, On Sects. This book explains different schools of medical thought: the different ways doctors tried to understand medicine.

last_spoken_paragraph: So far, we have heard Hunayn describe his work. A short medical saying will now let us see a thought moving between languages.
next_opening: The saying opens the Aphorisms, a collection of short medical statements linked with Hippocrates, an ancient Greek medical writer. Its first thought is simple: life is short, while learning the medical craft takes time.

last_spoken_paragraph: Yet a good translation on one person’s desk would not automatically put a book into another learner’s hands.
next_opening: Someone had to make that extra book. Each handwritten copy needed a writing surface, ink, a pen and a person able to use them. Knowing a text existed was different from being able to obtain it.

last_spoken_paragraph: Before ordering that work, a reader faced another question: which books existed, and which one should they ask for?
next_opening: Ibn al-Nadim, a Baghdad bookseller, helped readers answer that question. Around 987 or 988, he compiled the Fihrist, a large survey of books and their authors. It brought together work in many subjects and from different communities.

last_spoken_paragraph: The paper names lead beyond Baghdad, to the workshops and routes that kept writers supplied.
next_opening: Papermaking began in China. By around 800, paper was being made in Baghdad. Its journey involved both sheets that people could buy and skills that people could learn.

last_spoken_paragraph: A book by al-Khwārizmī will let us follow the difference between being given an answer and understanding why it works.
next_opening: Al-Khwārizmī worked in Baghdad in the 9th century, around the same time as Hunayn. His algebra book did more than give answers. It helped a learner see why a method worked. He named inheritance, trade and measuring land among its uses. Different everyday questions could share the same mathematical shape. Understanding one method could therefore help a learner solve another problem.

last_spoken_paragraph: The drawing has helped us check a calculation. But suppose the question is about something we see: why does light turn a picture upside down? We need to look at what light actually does.
next_opening: This room gives us a visible problem to explain. The bed is upright, but the outdoor building appears upside down on the wall. Its roof is below its windows. Most daylight has been blocked. A small opening admits enough light to form the image.

last_spoken_paragraph: Following light through a room is easier than explaining everything about human sight. It gives us one manageable part of the larger problem. But several paths enter through the same opening. We still need to ask whether they remain separate after they cross.
next_opening: Ibn al-Haytham describes several lamps outside a dark chamber. Their light passes through one opening and makes separate spots on the wall. Our drawing uses three lamps and three colours to help us follow their paths.

last_spoken_paragraph: The paths remain separate in the room. Now follow one into an eye. Where does its light arrive, and what part of the eye lets us see?
next_opening: Light can enter an eye, but that fact alone does not explain how we see. These pages show people working on that next problem. They kept useful questions from earlier writers while changing parts of the answer.

last_spoken_paragraph: A written explanation also has to work for someone who was not there to watch. Could a reader rebuild a device from its instructions? For that question, we step back from 1604 to 1206 and an engineer's clock.
next_opening: A clock has to do its job more than once. Announcing an interval is only half the problem. It must also get ready to start again. Al-Jazarī was an engineer for the Artuqid rulers in Diyarbakır, in today's Turkey. Their court supported the work of skilled makers. He completed his book of ingenious devices in 1206. The illustrated copy here was made later, in 1315.

last_spoken_paragraph: Al-Jazarī had a court behind his work. Books and lessons elsewhere also needed someone to provide materials and time. Let us move from the ruler's workshop to the people who supported students and teachers.
next_opening: A student needed more than a wish to learn. Someone had to provide a place, a book and a teacher's time. The stand, diploma and teaching records show different people taking care of those needs.

last_spoken_paragraph: A gift could support more than one lesson. What happened when people set aside income to keep a whole place of study running?
next_opening: In Cairo, Sultan Hasan's 14th-century complex used an endowment to support teachers and students. Income from property helped keep lessons and accommodation available.

last_spoken_paragraph: Supporting a teacher is one part of the job. What should the teacher teach first? A well-arranged book could help answer that question.
next_opening: Ibn Sīnā was a Muslim doctor and philosopher from Central Asia. In the early 11th century, he arranged a large body of medical knowledge into a book that teachers could use step by step.

last_spoken_paragraph: A course plan is still a large picture. What could a student learn on a particular page? Let us take two problems that need very little introduction.
next_opening: A broken bone is the first problem. This page, from a later English translation, describes bringing the separated parts together, supporting them with bandages and keeping the injured part still.

last_spoken_paragraph: Gerard translated this medical book, but his interests reached beyond medicine. In Toledo he also worked on an Arabic version of a famous astronomy book. There, checking the meaning of words was only part of the task.
next_opening: That book was the Almagest. Ptolemy, an astronomer working in Alexandria around 150, wrote it in Greek. Arabic scholars translated and studied it. Gerard then made it available in Latin.

last_spoken_paragraph: Tables put long calculations on a page. Astronomers also put mathematical relationships into an object they could carry outside and turn in their hands.
next_opening: This object is an astrolabe: a model of the sky that can be held in the hand. The maker, Muḥammad ibn al-Ṣaffār, worked in Toledo in 1029 or 1030. The thin tips of the open metalwork point to named stars.

last_spoken_paragraph: The photograph on the next page separates those layers. It will make the job of each part easier to see.
next_opening: Here is another astrolabe, displayed in Dresden with its parts apart. The case holds everything. A solid plate gives the local horizon. The open star map turns above it.

last_spoken_paragraph: A new owner may have the right plate and still face another problem: the writing on the instrument is in a language they cannot read.
next_opening: On this astrolabe, later readers added writing they could use. Made in 11th-century al-Andalus, in the Iberian Peninsula, it is now in Verona in Italy. Arabic engraving appears beside later Hebrew writing and Western numerals.

last_spoken_paragraph: An added label helps someone recognize a part. A learner who needs to operate the whole instrument also needs an explanation.
next_opening: Geoffrey Chaucer, the English poet, wrote a different kind of help in 1391. His Treatise on the Astrolabe addresses a boy called Lowys. The boy has an instrument for Oxford, wants to learn, and knows little Latin.

last_spoken_paragraph: Chaucer began with the needs of a particular learner. Almost 200 years earlier, another boy's education had connected an Italian family with the knowledge of a North African port.
next_opening: That boy was Leonardo of Pisa, better known as Fibonacci. His father worked with Pisan merchants in Béjaïa, in today's Algeria, and brought him there to learn calculation.

last_spoken_paragraph: Those Italian trading towns also supplied a material we have already met: paper. Its journey did not stop when it reached Europe.
next_opening: This Qur'an was copied around 1340 in Iraq or Iran on Italian paper. Earlier, we followed papermaking westwards through Islamic lands. Here, sheets travelled eastwards and became the surface for Qur'anic writing.

last_spoken_paragraph: We should also follow books beyond the Mediterranean ports. In West Africa, Muslim families built libraries around the subjects their own communities wanted to learn.
next_opening: Books also had long lives in Muslim communities far from the Mediterranean ports. Here we are in Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, south of the Sahara. Trade routes crossed there, and families built libraries for their own learning, worship and work.

last_spoken_paragraph: Nearby, in Djenne, people protect another inheritance by working on it together. Their mosque needs skills that each generation must learn.
next_opening: At Djenne, knowledge is also passed on through hands at work. Look at the mosque's earth walls, then compare the roof at Demak in Java, in present-day Indonesia. Both buildings serve a prayer familiar to us. Their shapes are different because their builders worked with different materials and local skills.

last_spoken_paragraph: Writers faced a similar question. How could something shared across the Muslim world also serve the language of a particular place?
next_opening: These pages show a similar kind of adaptation in writing. Both use Arabic-based letters, but one is in Malay and the other in Ottoman Turkish. Sharing letters does not make two languages the same. English and Turkish also share Latin letters, yet their words and grammar are different.

last_spoken_paragraph: We can now put the journeys together. What had to happen for knowledge to become useful in another community?
next_opening: At the start, we asked what happens when people need knowledge that someone else already has. The journeys have given us several answers. A useful idea does not reach a new reader through movement alone. People have to make it understandable, check it and help someone learn to use it.

last_spoken_paragraph: That leaves us with a prayer for the understanding we still hope to gain.
next_opening: Rabbi zidni ilma. My Lord, increase me in knowledge.

last_spoken_paragraph: We now have 5 minutes for your questions.
next_opening: Please raise your hand or write your question in the chat. We have 5 minutes together.
